claim: Spinal cord injury (SCI) causes devastating neurological impairments and disabilities.
source: Spinal cord injury (SCI) causes devastating neurological impairments and disabilities (Singh et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Singh et al., 2014

claim: SCI leads to the loss of sensory/motor functions and malfunctions in other organs such as bladder, kidneys and bowel.
source: SCI leads to the loss of sensory/motor functions and malfunctions in other organs such as bladder, kidneys and bowel, provoking an enormous impact on physical, psychological and social behavior of SCI patients (Bradbury and McMahon, 2006; Vismara et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bradbury and McMahon, 2006 and Vismara et al., 2017

claim: There is no fully restorative treatment for SCI yet.
source: Unfortunately, there is no fully restorative treatment for SCI yet (Silva et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Silva et al., 2014

claim: Medications or surgical decompression are the only options for SCI treatment.
source: Medications or surgical decompression are the only options for SCI treatment, however, these approaches are controversial due to the severe side effects and limited clinical efficacy (Cristante et al., 2012; Vismara et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cristante et al., 2012 and Vismara et al., 2017

claim: Cell replacement therapy has been proposed as a promising therapeutic intervention to reconstitute the damaged nervous system and improve functional recovery after SCI.
source: Thus, cell replacement therapy has been proposed as a promising therapeutic intervention to reconstitute the damaged nervous system and improve functional recovery after SCI (Goldman, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goldman, 2005

claim: Transplantation of neural cells derived from pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) is effective in functional and histological restoration in SCI animal model.
source: A number of studies have shown that transplantation of neural cells derived from pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) is effective in functional and histological restoration in SCI animal model (Lu et al., 2014; Nakamura and Okano, 2013; Tsuji et al., 2010; Vismara et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lu et al., 2014; Nakamura and Okano, 2013; Tsuji et al., 2010; Vismara et al., 2017

claim: Ethical issue of embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and tumorigenic potential of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) have impeded their translations into clinical trials.
source: Despite these encouraging advances, ethical issue of embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and tumorigenic potential of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) have impeded their translations into clinical trials (Deng et al., 2018; Fong et al., 2010; Miura et al., 2009; Ronaghi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deng et al., 2018; Fong et al., 2010; Miura et al., 2009; Ronaghi et al., 2010

claim: Direct conversion of somatic cells into other cell types has been achieved while bypassing pluripotent state.
source: To overcome these limitations, direct conversion of somatic cells into other cell types has been achieved while bypassing pluripotent state (Park et al., 2019; Park et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Park et al., 2019; Park et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2015

claim: Application of previous direct conversion protocols hindered therapeutic translations due to the heterogeneity and low yields, and involvement of multiple transcription factors which may increase the genetic mutagenesis.
source: However, application of previous protocols hindered therapeutic translations due to the heterogeneity and low yields, and involvement of multiple transcription factors which may increase the genetic mutagenesis (Kang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kang et al., 2015

claim: Directly converted cells are fully differentiated post-mitotic cells which limit the acquisition of cell source in large-scale for therapeutic purpose.
source: Most importantly, directly converted cells are fully differentiated post-mitotic cells which limit the acquisition of cell source in large-scale for therapeutic purpose.
evidence: This is a statement of limitation in the field based on established knowledge

claim: Human fibroblasts can be converted into induced motor neurons (iMNs) by sequentially inducing POU5F1(OCT4) and LHX3.
source: Here, we show that human fibroblasts can be converted into induced motor neurons (iMNs) by sequentially inducing POU5F1(OCT4) and LHX3.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript

claim: The sequential induction strategy enables scalable production of pure iMNs because of the transient acquisition of proliferative iMN-intermediate cell stage which is distinct from neural progenitors.
source: Our strategy enables scalable production of pure iMNs because of the transient acquisition of proliferative iMN-intermediate cell stage which is distinct from neural progenitors.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing proliferation and characterization of iMNICs

claim: iMNs exhibited hallmarks of spinal motor neurons including transcriptional profiles, electrophysiological property, synaptic activity, and neuromuscular junction formation.
source: iMNs exhibited hallmarks of spinal motor neurons including transcriptional profiles, electrophysiological property, synaptic activity, and neuromuscular junction formation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by multiple experimental data including RNA-seq, patch-clamp, immunostaining

claim: Transplantation of iMNs showed therapeutic effects, promoting locomotor functional recovery in rodent SCI model.
source: Remarkably, transplantation of iMNs showed therapeutic effects, promoting locomotor functional recovery in rodent SCI model.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in vivo transplantation data and BBB scoring

claim: POU5F1(OCT4) is known to play an important role in regulating pluripotent genes.
source: POU5F1(OCT4) is known to play an important role in regulating pluripotent genes (Shi and Jin, 2010; Wang et al., 2007), and downstream target genes involved in developmental processes (Shi and Jin, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shi and Jin, 2010; Wang et al., 2007

claim: Overexpression of POU5F1(OCT4) allowed the generation of blood progenitor cells from fibroblasts.
source: Previously, overexpression of POU5F1(OCT4) allowed the generation of blood progenitor cells from fibroblasts (Szabo et al., 2010) by regulating hematopoietic gene, HOXB4, which is one of the POU5F1(OCT4) targets (Boyer et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Szabo et al., 2010 and Boyer et al., 2005

claim: POU5F1(OCT4) can induce various cell fate reprogramming such as neural stem cells into iPSCs and fibroblasts into neural progenitor cells as well as oligodendrocyte progenitor cells.
source: Furthermore, a number of studies showed that POU5F1(OCT4) can induce various cell fate reprogramming such as neural stem cells into iPSCs (Kim et al., 2009a; Kim et al., 2009b), and fibroblasts into neural progenitor cells (Mitchell et al., 2014b) as well as oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (Kim et al., 2015), defining POU5F1(OCT4) as a versatile reprogramming factor that confers the plasticity in somatic cells (Mitchell et al., 2014a; Mitchell et al., 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2009a; Kim et al., 2009b; Mitchell et al., 2014b; Kim et al., 2015; Mitchell et al., 2014a

claim: POU5F1(OCT4) binds to homeodomain transcription factor ISL1.
source: Also, it has been reported that POU5F1(OCT4) binds to homeodomain transcription factor ISL1 (Boyer et al., 2005; Jung et al., 2010) which is required for specification of spinal cord MNs (Cho et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boyer et al., 2005; Jung et al., 2010

claim: ISL1 is required for specification of spinal cord MNs.
source: Also, it has been reported that POU5F1(OCT4) binds to homeodomain transcription factor ISL1 (Boyer et al., 2005; Jung et al., 2010) which is required for specification of spinal cord MNs (Cho et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cho et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2011

claim: None of the fibroblasts express neural lineage markers.
source: To rule out the possibility that resulting iMNs are derived from contaminating neural cells in parental fibroblasts, we confirmed that none of the fibroblasts express neural lineage markers by immunostaining with specific antibodies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: POU5F1(OCT4)-infected cells showed morphological changes as early as day 3, and spindle-shaped cells then formed compact colonies by day 10.
source: The morphological changes were observed as early as day 3, and spindle-shaped cells then formed compact colonies by day 10 (Figure 1C), whereas mock-infected fibroblasts did not change under the same condition (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images in Figure 1B and 1C

claim: From 0.5 × 10^4 seeded fibroblasts, 7 ~ 12 colonies could be observed.
source: From 0.5 × 104 seeded fibroblasts, we could observe 7 ~ 12 colonies (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Supplementary file 3

claim: The number of iMNIC cells increased over time in neural induction medium.
source: We found that the number of cells increased over time in neural induction medium.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments

claim: Six iMNIC clones were established from HF1: HF1-iMNIC2, HF1-iMNIC5, HF1-iMNIC6, HF1-iMNIC7, HF1-iMNIC11 and HF1-iMNIC12.
source: We could establish six iMNIC clones from HF1; HF1-iMNIC2, HF1-iMNIC5, HF1-iMNIC6, HF1-iMNIC7, HF1-iMNIC11 and HF1-iMNIC12 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by images in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and data in Supplementary file 3

claim: Only ISL1 was dramatically upregulated after POU5F1(OCT4) induction.
source: Notably, quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) analysis revealed that only ISL1 was dramatically upregulated after POU5F1(OCT4) induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: iMNICs robustly express ISL1, whereas other MN markers (HB9, NKX6.1 and LHX3) or neuronal markers (TUJ1 and MAP2) were not detected.
source: Consistently, immunocytochemistry also showed that iMNICs robustly express ISL1, whereas other MN markers (HB9, NKX6.1 and LHX3) or neuronal markers (TUJ1 and MAP2) were not detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C

claim: Addition of LHX3 to iMNICs enhanced conversion efficiency to generate HB9+TUJ1+ iMNs.
source: Addition of LHX3 to iMNICs but not any other MN factors enhanced conversion efficiency to generate HB9+TUJ1+ iMNs.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1H and quantification in Figure 1I-J

claim: More than 96% of iMNs co-expressed TUJ1 and HB9 in sphere culture.
source: More than 96% of iMNs co-expressed TUJ1 and HB9 in sphere culture, while the efficiency was considerably lower in adherent culture (Figure 1H–J and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 1J

claim: iMNIC clones were converted into HB9+TUJ1+ iMNs with conversion efficiency of 70 ~ 90%.
source: We applied this to other iMNIC clones, and they were converted into HB9+TUJ1+ iMNs with conversion efficiency of 70 ~ 90% (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B and Supplementary file 4

claim: None of iMNICs expressed early neuroectoderm markers (SOX1 and PAX6), neural progenitor markers (SOX2 and NCAM) or MN progenitor marker (OLIG2).
source: Immunocytochemistry analysis showed that none of iMNICs expressed early neuroectoderm markers (SOX1 and PAX6), neural progenitor markers (SOX2 and NCAM) or MN progenitor marker (OLIG2), and these markers were never detected during the entire neural induction process (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A

claim: None of pluripotent genes (POU5F1(OCT4) and NANOG) and neural progenitor marker (SOX2) were detected in POU5F1(OCT)-induced cells, iMNICs and iMNs.
source: We found that none of these markers were detected in POU5F1(OCT)-induced cells, iMNICs and iMNs as confirmed by qRT-PCR.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B

claim: Fibroblasts transit neither pluripotent state nor neural progenitor state during conversion to iMNs.
source: This result implies that fibroblasts transit neither pluripotent state nor neural progenitor state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gene expression data showing absence of pluripotent and neural progenitor markers

claim: iMNICs were highly proliferative cells and capable of being maintained for more than 13 passages.
source: Although iMNICs were distinct population from neural progenitors, these cells were highly proliferative cells and capable of being maintained for more than 13 passages.
evidence: Supported by proliferation data and passage experiments

claim: iMNICs sustained the proliferation rate presenting the mean doubling times (mDT) of 28.4 hr at P2 and 29.4 hr at P13.
source: The cells sustained the proliferation rate presenting the mean doubling times (mDT) of 28.4 hr at P2 and 29.4 hr at P13, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 5D).
evidence: Supported by proliferation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5D

claim: >97% of iMNICs expressed proliferative cell marker KI67.
source: In addition, we confirmed that >97% of iMNICs expressed proliferative cell marker KI67 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5E and F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5E and F

claim: iMNICs were successfully converted into mature iMNs at both early and late passage.
source: To verify the continuous capacity of iMNICs to convert into iMNs over multiple passages, we conducted iMN induction using iMNICs at P2 and P13. iMNICs were successfully converted into mature iMNs at both early and late passage (Figure 1—figure supplement 5G).
evidence: Supported by conversion efficiency data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5G

claim: When fibroblasts were infected with POU5F1(OCT4) and LHX3 simultaneously, the majority of infected cells died and iMNIC colonies were not stably maintained for multiple passages after picking (up to 5 passages).
source: When we infected fibroblasts with POU5F1(OCT4) and LHX3 simultaneously, the majority of infected cells died and iMNIC colonies were not stably maintained for multiple passages after picking (up to 5 passages) (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: Supported by morphology and survival data in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A

claim: Proliferation rate and ISL1 gene expression were decreased in POU5F1(OCT4)/LHX3 induced iMNICs compared to POU5F1(OCT4)-induced iMNICs.
source: Proliferation rate and ISL1 gene expression were also decreased in POU5F1(OCT4)/LHX3 induced iMNICs compared to POU5F1(OCT4)-induced iMNICs (Figure 1—figure supplement 6B and C).
evidence: Supported by proliferation and qRT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 6B and C

claim: Induction of POU5F1(OCT4) alone showed higher efficiency in the number of iMNIC colonies.
source: In addition, induction of POU5F1(OCT4) alone showed higher efficiency in the number of iMNIC colonies (Figure 1—figure supplement 6D).
evidence: Supported by colony counting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 6D

claim: The sequential induction of two transcription factors is essential for generating self-renewing iMNICs more efficiently.
source: These data indicate that the sequential induction of two transcription factors is essential for generating self-renewing iMNICs more efficiently.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison data between sequential and simultaneous induction

claim: HB9:GFP+ iMNs co-expressed MN markers including NKX6.1, ISL1, HB9 and CHAT as well as neuronal markers, TUJ1 and MAP2.
source: Immunocytochemistry analysis showed that HB9:GFP+ iMNs co-expressed MN markers including NKX6.1, ISL1, HB9 and CHAT as well as neuronal markers, TUJ1 and MAP2 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 2B

claim: Tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive dopaminergic neurons were rare in population (<0.6%).
source: In contrast, tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive dopaminergic neurons were rare in population (<0.6%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and GFAP-positive astrocytes were not detected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that our reprogramming method is specific to MN lineage rather than other neuronal subtypes or neural progenitors.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: GFAP-positive astrocytes were not detected in iMNs.
source: In contrast, tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive dopaminergic neurons were rare in population (<0.6%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and GFAP-positive astrocytes were not detected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that our reprogramming method is specific to MN lineage rather than other neuronal subtypes or neural progenitors.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: The reprogramming method is specific to MN lineage rather than other neuronal subtypes or neural progenitors.
source: In contrast, tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive dopaminergic neurons were rare in population (<0.6%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and GFAP-positive astrocytes were not detected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that our reprogramming method is specific to MN lineage rather than other neuronal subtypes or neural progenitors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low/absent expression of non-MN markers

claim: The endogenous mRNA levels of MN marker genes including LIM1, LHX3, NKX6.1, HB9 and ISL1 were upregulated in iMNs relative to fibroblasts.
source: Consistent with the immunocytochemistry results, the endogenous mRNA levels of MN marker genes including LIM1, LHX3, NKX6.1, HB9 and ISL1 were upregulated in iMNs relative to fibroblasts (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2C

claim: Synaptic activities of HB9:GFP+ neurites expressing presynaptic markers, SYN1 and synaptic vesicle protein 2 (SV2) were observed.
source: Furthermore, we could observe the synaptic activities of HB9:GFP+ neurites expressing presynaptic markers, SYN1 and synaptic vesicle protein 2 (SV2) (Figure 2D,E and Figure 1—figure supplement 5H).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2D, E and Figure 1—figure supplement 5H

claim: Exogenous expression of transgenes POU5F1(OCT4) and LHX3 are dramatically decreased in iMNs.
source: We next confirmed the transgene silencing in iMNs. Exogenous expression of transgenes POU5F1(OCT4) and LHX3 are dramatically decreased in iMNs, as examined by qRT-PCR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D

claim: 29 out of 48 tested cells (60.42%) exhibited at least one action potential (AP) firing.
source: 29 out of 48 tested cells (60.42%) exhibited at least one action potential (AP) firing, while 19 cells (39.58%) were unresponsive to depolarizing current injection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: About half of the cells showing AP (14 cells) generated a multiple number of AP firings and 8 out of 14 cells also showed spontaneous firing at resting membrane potential.
source: Among the cells showing AP (29 cells), about half of the cells (14 cells) generated a multiple number of AP firings and 8 out of 14 cells also showed spontaneous firing at resting membrane potential (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: There were no significant differences in AP threshold, frequency, amplitude, half-width and neuronal excitability between group 1 and group 2 iMNs.
source: Likewise, there were no significant differences in AP threshold, frequency, amplitude, half-width and neuronal excitability between the two groups (Figure 3F–J), suggesting that these cells are functionally matured regardless of spontaneous firing at resting membrane potential.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data and statistical analysis in Figure 3F-J

claim: iMNs are functionally matured regardless of spontaneous firing at resting membrane potential.
source: Likewise, there were no significant differences in AP threshold, frequency, amplitude, half-width and neuronal excitability between the two groups (Figure 3F–J), suggesting that these cells are functionally matured regardless of spontaneous firing at resting membrane potential.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological characterization data

claim: Inward currents in iMNs were completely blocked by the bath-application of tetrodotoxin (TTX).
source: In voltage clamp mode, depolarizing voltage steps also induced fast inward currents. These currents were completely blocked by the bath-application of tetrodotoxin (TTX). We confirmed that these inward currents were elicited by TTX-sensitive voltage-gated sodium channels (Figure 3K–M).
evidence: Supported by voltage clamp data in Figure 3K-M

claim: Inward currents in iMNs were elicited by TTX-sensitive voltage-gated sodium channels.
source: In voltage clamp mode, depolarizing voltage steps also induced fast inward currents. These currents were completely blocked by the bath-application of tetrodotoxin (TTX). We confirmed that these inward currents were elicited by TTX-sensitive voltage-gated sodium channels (Figure 3K–M).
evidence: Supported by voltage clamp data showing TTX sensitivity in Figure 3K-M

claim: iMNs are electrophysiologically mature.
source: Together, these data indicate that iMNs are electrophysiologically mature.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comprehensive electrophysiological characterization

claim: Extensive axons of HB9:GFP+ iMNs projected along the myotubes.
source: Extensive axons of HB9:GFP+ iMNs projected along the myotubes (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 4A

claim: SV2-positive vesicles were seen in HB9:GFP+ iMNs and enriched at NMJs showing puncta-like structures.
source: Noticeably, SV2-positive vesicles were seen in HB9:GFP+ iMNs and enriched at NMJs showing puncta-like structures (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 4A

claim: Clusters of postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors (AChR) on the surface of myotubes were detected at the sites of contacts with myotubes.
source: At the sites of contacts with myotubes, clusters of postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors (AChR) on the surface of myotubes were detected by immunocytochemistry with AChR antibody (Figure 4B) and α-bungarotoxin conjugated with Alexa 555 (α-BTX) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 4B and 4C

claim: Rhythmic contraction of myotubes was observed when co-cultured with iMNs.
source: Importantly, we could observe the rhythmic contraction of myotubes when co-cultured with iMNs. The contractions were blocked by antagonist of nicotinic AChR, curare, indicating that the myotubes contract depending on the activities of iMNs (Video 1).
evidence: Supported by video recording in Video 1

claim: The myotubes contract depending on the activities of iMNs.
source: Importantly, we could observe the rhythmic contraction of myotubes when co-cultured with iMNs. The contractions were blocked by antagonist of nicotinic AChR, curare, indicating that the myotubes contract depending on the activities of iMNs (Video 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the curare blocking experiment

claim: Mature iMNs exhibit mature functionality such as the formation of NMJs.
source: These data demonstrate that mature iMNs exhibit mature functionality such as the formation of NMJs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NMJ formation and contraction data

claim: HF2-derived iMNs (HF2-iMNs) showed typical characteristics of MNs and functions, such as synaptic activities and NMJ formation.
source: HF2-derived iMNs (HF2-iMNs) showed typical characteristics of MNs and functions, such as synaptic activities and NMJ formation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D

claim: Five iMNIC clones were established from HF2: HF2-iMNIC1, HF2-iMNIC2, HF2-iMNIC4, HF2-iMNIC6 and HF2-iMNIC8.
source: We could establish five iMNIC clones from HF2; HF2-iMNIC1, HF2-iMNIC2, HF2-iMNIC4, HF2-iMNIC6 and HF2-iMNIC8) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by morphology images in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E

claim: HF2-derived iMNIC clones highly expressed ISL1 gene.
source: These iMNIC clones highly expressed ISL1gene, and the cells were converted into HB9+iMNs after MN induction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F

claim: HF2-derived iMNIC clones were converted into HB9+iMNs after MN induction.
source: These iMNIC clones highly expressed ISL1gene, and the cells were converted into HB9+iMNs after MN induction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by GFP imaging in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G

claim: iMN conversion method is applicable to other lines of human adult fibroblasts.
source: Taken together, these results confirm that iMN conversion method is applicable to other lines of human adult fibroblasts.
evidence: This is an inference based on successful conversion from HF2 fibroblasts

claim: The global gene expression patterns of iMNICs and iMNs were similar to wtMNs, but distinct from fibroblasts and fetal NPCs.
source: Heatmap analysis demonstrated that the global gene expression patterns of iMNICs and iMNs were similar to wtMNs, but distinct from fibroblasts and fetal NPCs (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by heatmap analysis in Figure 5A

claim: iMNICs, iMNs and wtMNs are tightly correlated in hierarchical clustering and principal component analysis.
source: The hierarchical clustering and principal component analysis (PCA) showed that iMNICs, iMNs and wtMNs are tightly correlated, whereas distinct from NSCs (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by hierarchical clustering in Figure 5B and PCA in Figure 5C

claim: The 1st principal component (PC1) captures 39% of the gene expression variability and the 2nd principal component (PC2) captures 26% of the variability.
source: The 1st principal component (PC1) captures 39% of the gene expression variability and the 2nd principal component (PC2) captures 26% of the variability.
evidence: This is a result from PCA analysis

claim: Pairwise scatter plots showed high similarity between iMNICs vs fetal spinal cord and iMNs vs wtMNs, especially in HOX genes and MN-enriched genes.
source: Moreover, pairwise scatter plots showed high similarity between iMNICs vs fetal spinal cord and iMNs vs wtMNs, especially in HOX genes (HOXC4, HOXC6, HOXC8, HOXC9, HOXA9 and HOXD9) and MN-enriched genes (HB9, ISL1, NKX6.1, TUJ1, MAP2 and CHAT) (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by scatter plot analysis in Figure 5D

claim: Low similarity was observed between iMNICs vs NPC and parental fibroblasts vs iMNICs/iMNs, especially in NPC marker genes and fibroblast genes.
source: In contrast, we could observe low similarity between iMNICs vs NPC and parental fibroblasts vs iMNICs/iMNs, especially NPC marker genes (SOX2, OLIG2, PAX6 and SOX1) and fibroblast genes (COL5A1 and COL1A1) (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by scatter plot analysis in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: High level of similarity in HOX gene clusters and MN genes was observed in iMNICs and iMNs compared to wtMNs, which were not expressed in NPCs.
source: Furthermore, we could observe high level of similarity in HOX gene clusters and MN genes in our iMNICs and iMNs compared to wtMNs, which were not expressed in NPCs (Figure 5E,F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by heatmap analysis in Figure 5E, F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: The expression of NPC genes (SOX2, PAX6, OLIG2, ASCL1, FABP7 and EMX), fibroblast-specific genes (COL1A1, COL5A1, SNA1 and SNAI2) and pluripotent genes (NANOG, POU5F1(OCT4) and TDGF1) were not detectable in iMNICs and iMNs.
source: In contrast, the expression of NPC genes (SOX2, PAX6, OLIG2, ASCL1, FABP7 and EMX), fibroblast-specific genes (COL1A1, COL5A1, SNA1 and SNAI2) and pluripotent genes (NANOG, POU5F1(OCT4) and TDGF1) were not detectable in iMNICs and iMNs (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by heatmap analysis in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: Cervical and thoracic spinal cord specific genes (HOX4-9) were upregulated in iMNICs and iMNs.
source: Consistent with RNA-sequencing data, cervical and thoracic spinal cord specific genes (HOX4-9) were upregulated in iMNICs and iMNs as confirmed by qRT-PCR (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5G

claim: iMNs generated from two fibroblast lines acquired motor neuronal identity and showed a high degree of similarity with wtMNs or fetal spinal cord tissues.
source: Together, these results indicate that iMNs generated from two fibroblast lines acquired motor neuronal identity and showed a high degree of similarity with wtMNs or fetal spinal cord tissues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comprehensive RNA-seq analysis

claim: Engraftment of transplanted HB9:GFP+ iMNs in the spinal cord was observed.
source: We could observe the engraftment of transplanted HB9:GFP+ iMNs in the spinal cord (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 6B

claim: Most of the GFP+ cells co-expressed TUJ1 in vivo.
source: Most of the GFP+ cells co-expressed TUJ1 (Figure 6C–E) and were surrounded by host myelinating MBP+ oligodendrocytes (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging in Figure 6C-E

claim: Transplanted iMNs were surrounded by host myelinating MBP+ oligodendrocytes.
source: Most of the GFP+ cells co-expressed TUJ1 (Figure 6C–E) and were surrounded by host myelinating MBP+ oligodendrocytes (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging in Figure 6F-H

claim: Transplanted tissue show less cavity of injured site compared to control.
source: Transplanted tissue show less cavity of injured site compared to control (Figure 6I and J).
evidence: Supported by H&E staining in Figure 6I and J

claim: iMN-transplanted rats were improved in BBB scores from week 4 that persisted steadily through week 8 showing significant improvement in locomotor recovery.
source: iMN-transplanted rats were improved in BBB scores from week 4 that persisted steadily through week showing significant improvement in locomotor recovery (Figure 6K,L and Video 2).
evidence: Supported by BBB scoring data in Figure 6K, L and Video 2

claim: No tumors were observed for 12 months after subcutaneous transplantation of iMNICs and iMNs into immune-deficient nude mice.
source: To assess the risk of tumor formation, iMNICs and iMNs were subcutaneously transplanted into immune-deficient nude mice and no tumors were observed for 12 months of experiment period (n = 4) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by long-term observation data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A

claim: iMN transplantation significantly improved functional recovery after SCI.
source: These results showed that iMN transplantation significantly improved functional recovery after SCI.
evidence: This is an inference based on the BBB scoring and histological data

claim: POU5F1(OCT4) can initiate cellular reprogramming toward MN lineage by activating ISL1.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first time showing that POU5F1(OCT4) can initiate cellular reprogramming toward MN lineage by activating ISL1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ISL1 is activated after POU5F1(OCT4) induction

claim: The LIM complex composed of ISL1 and LHX3 specify spinal MNs by inducing MN gene HB9 in development.
source: This result is consistent with the previous report that the LIM complex composed of ISL1 and LHX3 specify spinal MNs by inducing MN gene HB9 in development (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2012

claim: iMNs were generated by either eight transcription factors (ASCL1, BRN2, MYT1L, LHX3, HB9, ISL1, NGN2, and NEUROD1) in previous studies.
source: Previously, iMNs were generated by either eight transcription factors (ASCL1, BRN2, MYT1L, LHX3, HB9, ISL1, NGN2, and NEUROD1) (Son et al., 2011) or four transcription factors (NGN2, SOX11, ISL1, and LHX3) (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Son et al., 2011 and Liu et al., 2016

claim: Previous studies have not verified the in vivo functionality or therapeutic potential of human iMNs.
source: Moreover, previous studies have not verified the in vivo functionality or therapeutic potential of human iMNs.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field

claim: iMNs exhibited transcriptional profiles of motor neuronal identity similar with wtMNs.
source: In addition, RNA-sequencing analysis revealed that our iMNs exhibited transcriptional profiles of motor neuronal identity similar with wtMNs.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis data

claim: iMNICs and iMNs expressed spinal cord specific HOX5-9 gene clusters.
source: Importantly, iMNICs and iMNs expressed spinal cord specific HOX5-9 gene clusters, whereas NPC genes were not detected in these cells.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and qRT-PCR data

claim: NPC genes were not detected in iMNICs and iMNs.
source: Importantly, iMNICs and iMNs expressed spinal cord specific HOX5-9 gene clusters, whereas NPC genes were not detected in these cells.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and immunostaining data

claim: Previous direct conversion methods have not been feasible since directly converted neurons are terminally differentiated cells that are not scalable.
source: However, previous methods have not been feasible since directly converted neurons are terminally differentiated cells that are not scalable.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations in the field based on established knowledge

claim: Neural progenitors could produce a mixture of heterogeneous neurons.
source: This limitation could be overcome by generating expandable neural progenitors; however, neural progenitors could produce a mixture of heterogeneous neurons (Lujan et al., 2012; Ring et al., 2012; Thier et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lujan et al., 2012; Ring et al., 2012; Thier et al., 2012

claim: Sequential introduction of two transcription factors enabled the large production of pure iMNs.
source: Herein, sequential introduction of two transcription factors enabled the large production of pure iMNs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study

claim: iMNICs were proliferative, expandable and retained conversion capacity to mature iMNs for long-term culture (>13 passages).
source: iMNICs were proliferative, expandable and retained conversion capacity to mature iMNs for long-term culture (>13 passages); however, they were distinct from neural progenitors.
evidence: Supported by proliferation assays and conversion efficiency data

claim: The method is 'direct conversion' rather than indirect conversion or redifferentiation through pluripotent state or neural progenitor state.
source: Therefore, our method is 'direct conversion' rather than indirect conversion or redifferentiation through pluripotent state or neural progenitor state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of pluripotent and neural progenitor markers

claim: Mitchell et al. generated iNPC from POU5F1(OCT4)-induced fibroblasts by culturing the cells in reprogramming media (RM) for 8 days before inducing in classical NPC media.
source: Previously, Mitchell et al. generated iNPC from POU5F1(OCT4)-induced fibroblasts by culturing the cells in reprogramming media (RM) for 8 days before inducing in classical NPC media (Mitchell et al., 2014a; Mitchell et al., 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mitchell et al., 2014a; Mitchell et al., 2014b

claim: RM step is essential to induce SOX2+ NPCs after POU5F1(OCT4) induction according to Mitchell et al.
source: They reported that RM step is essential to induce SOX2+ NPCs after POU5F1(OCT4) induction.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from Mitchell et al.

claim: SOX2 was not activated in POU5F1(OCT4)-infected cells and failed to generate iNPCs when cultured directly in NPC media according to Mitchell et al.
source: In contrast, SOX2 was not activated in POU5F1(OCT4)-infected cells and failed to generate iNPCs when cultured directly in NPC media (Mitchell et al., 2014a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mitchell et al., 2014a

claim: iMNICs which were generated without RM step did not express neural progenitor marker.
source: Consistent with previous report by Mitchell et al., our iMNICs which were generated without RM step did not express neural progenitor marker (Mitchell et al., 2014a; Mitchell et al., 2014b).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and gene expression data

claim: Extracellular environment and timing for appropriate stimuli are critical for cell identification of POU5F1(OCT4)-induced cells.
source: This finding indicates that extracellular environment and timing for appropriate stimuli are critical for cell identification of POU5F1(OCT4)-induced cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison with Mitchell et al.'s findings

claim: Transplantation of MNs or MN precursors differentiated from pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) showed functional benefits to injured spinal cord.
source: Several studies have reported that transplantation of MNs or MN precursors differentiated from pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) showed functional benefits to injured spinal cord (Rossi et al., 2010; Wyatt et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rossi et al., 2010; Wyatt et al., 2011

claim: Translation of PSC-derived cells to the clinic is limited due to challenges including differentiation efficiency, scalability, purity, and especially tumorigenecity from undifferentiated cells.
source: However, translation of these cells to the clinic is limited due to the challenges including differentiation efficiency, scalability, purity, and especially tumorigenecity from undifferentiated cells (Nori et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nori et al., 2015

claim: Transplantation of MN precursors remain poorly defined because of stem cell heterogeneity.
source: Moreover, transplantation of MN precursors remain poorly defined because of stem cell heterogeneity (Trawczynski et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Trawczynski et al., 2019

claim: Hindlimb functional recovery depends on maturity and purity of iMNs.
source: In this study, we could obtain pure iMNs in large number and found that hindlimb functional recovery depends on maturity and purity of iMNs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between iMN spheres and selected HB9+ iMNs

claim: When selected HB9+ mature iMNs were transplanted, BBB score was higher compared to transplanting iMN spheres.
source: When we transplanted selected HB9+ mature iMNs, BBB score was higher compared to transplanting iMN spheres.
evidence: Supported by BBB scoring data in Figure 6L

claim: Transplanted HB9+ iMNs still expressed neuronal markers and interacted with host neural cells such as oligodendrocytes in vivo.
source: We also observed that our iMNs exhibited integration properties when transplanted into injured spinal cord. Transplanted HB9+ iMNs still expressed neuronal markers and interacted with host neural cells such as oligodendrocytes in vivo.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in vivo

claim: Ensheathment by myelinating host oligodendrocytes surrounding iMNs was observed.
source: We could observe ensheathment by myelinating host oligodendrocytes surrounding our iMNs.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging in Figure 6F-H

claim: Transplantation of iMNs contributed histological and functional recovery in SCI model without tumor formation.
source: Notably, transplantation of iMNs contributed histological and functional recovery in SCI model without tumor formation, and this is the first report demonstrating the therapeutic effects of human iMNs in vivo.
evidence: Supported by H&E staining, BBB scoring, and tumor formation assay data

claim: This is the first report demonstrating the therapeutic effects of human iMNs in vivo.
source: Notably, transplantation of iMNs contributed histological and functional recovery in SCI model without tumor formation, and this is the first report demonstrating the therapeutic effects of human iMNs in vivo.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings

claim: Functional iMNs can be employed to cell-based therapy as an autologous cell source.
source: In conclusion, this proof-of-concept study shows that our functional iMNs can be employed to cell-based therapy as an autologous cell source.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications based on the study findings

claim: iMNs possessed spinal cord motor neuronal identity.
source: iMNs possessed spinal cord motor neuronal identity and exhibit hallmarks of spinal MNs such as neuromuscular junction formation capacity and electrophysiological properties in vitro.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq, immunostaining, and functional assay data

claim: Transplantation of iMNs improved locomotor function in rodent SCI model without tumor formation.
source: Importantly, transplantation of iMNs improved locomotor function in rodent SCI model without tumor formation.
evidence: Supported by BBB scoring and tumor formation assay data

claim: The strategy is a safer and simpler methodology that may provide new insights to develop personalized stem cell therapy and drug screening for MN diseases or spinal cord disorders.
source: Although further investigation on mechanism responsible for cell fate conversion may be needed, our strategy is a safer and simpler methodology that may provide new insights to develop personalized stem cell therapy and drug screening for MN diseases or spinal cord disorders.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications and implications
